Question: if there was a mirror with 1 square kilometer area in space that covers the same field of view as Hubble, how sharp would galaxies 10 billion light years away look?

Assuming you meant 1km across. The mirrors used in telescopes are circular and measured in the diameter.

Simple answer: 417 times sharper than the Hubble

The Hubble mirror is 2.4 meters wide so divide 1000 by that and you get the increase in clarity.

Complex answer: To be able to see a galaxy (which has wavelengths of light) it is a simple formula to determine telescope mirror size vs. smallest viewable angle of said galaxy.

Theta = Lambda/D

In this Theta is represented by the distance between two points or the smallest resolvable angle of the galaxy you are trying to view. Lambda represents the wavelength of the thing you are trying to view. In this case it will take the value of 5e-7 meters as that is the wave length of visible light. D is the diameter of the telescope mirror.

So to determine the minimum mirror size to see light 10 billion light years away. That means first finding the smallest resolvable angle. This is done with the following equation.

Theta=S/L

Here Theta again represents the distance between two points or the smallest resolvable angle of the galaxy you are trying to view. S is the size of the object you are trying to view. And L is the distance of that object trying to be viewed.

The distance is 10 billion light years or 6e+22 miles (6 Trillion miles to a light year). Taking the size of our own Galaxy we find S to be 6e+17 miles.

So calculate that out and you get .00001 degree for the smallest resolvable angle.

Input that now into our other formula to find the minimum mirror diameter to see the said object. You then get .05 meters. So the Hubble is 2.4 meters in diameter and the minimum needed to see that object that far away is about 2 meters less. This should give you an idea of how much clearer a picture a 1km diameter mirrored telescope could provide.

Edit: Word order in simple answer section
So does that mean that near the cosmic microwave background, you could see details that are just 10 light years across?

Well lets do some more number crunching...

Taking again the formula to determine the smallest resolvable angle for an object 10 light years across at the distance of the cosmic microwave background (Using 45 Billion light years).

Theta=S/L

S is equal to 10 light years or 6e+13 miles. L is equal to 45 billion light years or 2.7e+23 miles. Calculate and you get the smallest resolvable angle as .0000000002 degrees.

Pop that number into our other equation...

Theta=Lambda/D

Here Theta is .0000000002 degrees. Lambda again will be the wave length for visible light at 5e-7 meters. Calculate it out and you will get an answer of 2500 meters or 2.5km diameter mirror to be able to view visible light 10 light years across at the cosmic microwave background.

Now consider however that Lambda in this case could vary quite a lot depending on the data you are trying to collect. Since the Cosmic microwave background is just that "a background", it consists of many different forms of radiation which all have their own wave length's. So whichever piece of data you are looking for that value would be variable. Also finding certain wavelengths is not as simple as pointing a telescope with the proper resolution and presto you can see it. Most non-visible frequencies of radiation need special equipment to properly view.
Thanks. I wonder if 2.5km mirror would be able to detect Earth-like exoplanets directly.

Well using those same formulas you can determine how effective it would be. It would require slightly more math to determine how high a resolution you could get, but nothing too complicated. The problem with viewing Earth-Like Exoplanets or Exoplanets in general is capturing enough light to get a clear picture of the planet. Since they are usually pretty far away the light that reflects off the Exoplanet is minimal. This means that the telescope needs to look at the planet for a longer period of time. And if the planet is anything like Earth it will mean that it has a rotation on its own axis and one around it's star. Therefore observing for a longer period to take in more light and provide a better picture, actually makes it harder to view since the amount of light will be constantly varying and the object is moving in multiple ways. Would love to see technology and science overcome this though.
